items.title: [elpais.com] Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems fuel concerns about connected household appliances
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Cyberattacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems in supermarkets and French blood banks have destroyed food in Europe and heightened concerns about connected devices. Nearly 800 freezers were sabotaged in France and Northern Europe this week. On November 2, temperatures also rose in the cold rooms of a blood donation service in France. There, alarms and swift action prevented damage to stored blood. The targeted systems used internet-accessible controls for maintenance and remote operation. According to experts, similar attacks on private smart-home devices are less likely because, with typical router configurations, the devices cannot be accessed directly from the internet. Risks include outdated software, weak passwords, and devices with cameras or microphones. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security recommends automatic updates, separate networks for smart-home devices, and unique passwords. The identity of those behind the attacks remains unclear.

items.title: [e.vnexpress.net] Travel technology provider Amadeus breach exposes 46,000 Singapore Airlines records
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Singapore Airlines said about 46,000 booking records may have been accessed in a breach at travel technology provider Amadeus, potentially exposing passenger names, booking references, itineraries and booking classes. About 620 records may also have included email addresses, phone numbers, travel-document details and KrisFlyer membership numbers. The airline said payment information was not exposed, bookings were not changed and its own systems were not breached. The unauthorized access involved booking data from August 2023 to September 2026. Cathay Pacific reported about 53,000 affected bookings, Japan Airlines about 92,000 affected customers and All Nippon Airways 37,800 affected records; Qantas is still checking whether its bookings were affected. Amadeus said it fixed the vulnerability and strengthened monitoring. Singapore Airlines is contacting customers with upcoming travel to change their booking references, while Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Commission said it is investigating.

items.title: [space.com] Simulations link Uranus and Neptune’s skewed magnetic fields to interior conditions
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Computer simulations based on Voyager 2 measurements suggest that increasing electrical conductivity with depth inside Uranus and Neptune may explain their unusually tilted, off-center magnetic fields. The study, led by Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin, was published Nov. 3 in Communications Physics. The models indicate that the fields may also shift substantially over decades, unlike Earth’s comparatively steady magnetic tilt. Researchers are using observations of faint auroras from the James Webb Space Telescope to track the planets’ magnetic environments; NASA has prioritized a Uranus mission for the early 2040s.

The model’s exploit-development abilities can support security testing or be used in attacks. Anthropic said its AI research and development has reached a safety-policy threshold tied to AI accelerating its own progress. The maker of Claude disclosed the determination in an amended filing as it began marketing its planned initial public offering (IPO). The offering would be one of the first public listings by a leading AI model developer. Anthropic said it based the determination on expectations for future models and its overall rate of progress, not on behavior observed in current models. items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

An attack on a refrigeration service provider used by France’s national blood service reached monitoring and control systems at three sites on Nov. 2. The blood service said it was not directly targeted. Investigators have not publicly identified how attackers entered the contractor’s systems, which control equipment was affected or who was responsible. French reporting said attackers set controls to request temperatures as high as 110°C, but that figure does not establish the temperatures reached inside storage units or blood products. European retailers have also faced attacks on internet-connected refrigeration controls. Interface cybersecurity adviser Sven Herpig said the supermarket attacks exploited weak or known credentials and a lack of multi-factor authentication, while another security expert pointed to default passwords and outdated systems. Investigators have not confirmed that the blood-storage attack exploited the same weaknesses or was linked to the retail incidents. The European Commission, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and other EU bodies advised organizations to act immediately to reduce exposure and are sharing information with national authorities. Under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, manufacturers have been required to report severe incidents and actively exploited vulnerabilities since Sept. 11, 2026. Its main security requirements take effect Dec. 11, 2027.

items.title: [farmer.pl] Farmers urged to shred corn stalks to curb pests and disease
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

As Poland’s corn harvest continues, agronomic guidance recommends finely shredding stalks and other crop residues after harvest to reduce winter shelter for the European corn borer and limit disease in the next season. The borer’s larvae overwinter in stalks, while feeding damage can promote Fusarium infections that contaminate grain with mycotoxins. Residue management also affects soil organic matter: grain corn leaves substantial biomass in the field, while silage harvesting removes nearly all above-ground material. Guidance recommends accounting for soil moisture and the next crop; working wet soil can cause compaction, and fields vulnerable to erosion may need residue left on the surface.
